content:
Right now Module.restrictScalars R S S, Module.restrictScalars R R S and
Algebra.toModule: Module R S are not defeq at implicit reducibility. This is cause by
RingHom.comp and algebraMap both being semireducible. More generally, throughout Mathlib there
are (an unknown number of) instances that were relying on non-instance definitions being reduced.
In the case of definitions that return a class, these have all been made implicit_reducible, but
there isn't consensus to do the same for these structure returning definitions. For example,
this post by Eric Wieser: https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/113488-general/topic/backward.2EisDefEq.2ErespectTransparency/near/581509978

The other options which have been proposed or which I can think of are:

  • Rewrite the instances to use { RingHom.comp _ _ with toFun = _} and use Algebra.algebraMap directly.
  • Create an elaborator to do the same: https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/113488-general/topic/backward.2EisDefEq.2ErespectTransparency/near/581510125

  • Create implicit_reducible helper definitions that are otherwise the same as RingHom.comp,
    algebraMap, etc.

  • Make Algebra.algebraMap and similar bump the reducibility to default: https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/287929-mathlib4/topic/backward.2EisDefEq.2ErespectTransparency.3A.20Algebra.20.E2.84.9D.20.E2.84.82.20issues/near/579404514

  • Keep the diamonds and use simp and/or IsScalarTower like instances to handle them.

None of these seem more appealing to me than making the definitions implicit_reducible right now.
The answers to the following questions might change my mind though:

  • How many definitions would be tagged if we took this approach all similar diamonds?

  • Do definitions that don't have to be implicit_reducible for an actual diamond, but are similar
    to those that do get marked? We might either have inconsistent use of the attribute, or end up
    with a lot of implicit_reducible definitions.

  • What is the performance impact?

  • Does this lead to any cases where things are defeq at reducible transparency when we don't
    want them to be?
See #mathlib4 > backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency: Algebra ℝ ℂ issues for some previous discussion

Matthew Jasper said:

  • Rewrite the instances to use { RingHom.comp _ _ with toFun = _} and use Algebra.algebraMap directly.
  • Create implicit_reducible helper definitions that are otherwise the same as RingHom.comp,

I'm not sure what is the problem with either of these ideas. They both seem reasonable to me.

Matthew Jasper said:

  • Make Algebra.algebraMap and similar bump the reducibility to default: https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/287929-mathlib4/topic/backward.2EisDefEq.2ErespectTransparency.3A.20Algebra.20.E2.84.9D.20.E2.84.82.20issues/near/579404514
  • Keep the diamonds and use simp and/or IsScalarTower like instances to handle them.

These, on the other hand, seem like a bad idea to me.

Jireh Loreaux said:

Matthew Jasper said:

  • Rewrite the instances to use { RingHom.comp _ _ with toFun = _} and use Algebra.algebraMap directly.
  • Create implicit_reducible helper definitions that are otherwise the same as RingHom.comp,

I'm not sure what is the problem with either of these ideas. They both seem reasonable to me.

I think that they're fine if there's agreement to do them.

Note that you seemed to suggest otherwise, which was the reason I phrase my response that way:
Matthew Jasper said:

None of these seem more appealing to me than making the definitions implicit_reducible right now.
A related change we could consider in isolation is dropping docs#algebraMap entirely and using export Algebra (algebraMap) instead (attempted in #37401)
Existing callers wouldn't know the difference, but the map would end up with a longer full name

Jireh Loreaux said:

Matthew Jasper said:

  • Make Algebra.algebraMap and similar bump the reducibility to default: https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/287929-mathlib4/topic/backward.2EisDefEq.2ErespectTransparency.3A.20Algebra.20.E2.84.9D.20.E2.84.82.20issues/near/579404514

Th[is], on the other hand, seem[s] like a bad idea to me.

Could you elaborate on this? Is the badness just "this requires effort in lean core", or also the end state of having some fields use different reducibility rules to others?
Yes, I think such reducibility changes would be incredibly confusing.
Isn't it also confusing to have the requirement that "every bundled morphism / structure of any kind in a typeclass must be implemented as a constructor application"?

That is not the requirement. Instead, this is only required for those parts that need to have certain defeq properties. I don't see why this is confusing, as all instances already have this requirement anyways.
Sorry, I meant "implemented as reducibly a constructor application"
Maybe its worth doing some quick analysis of how many typeclasses have fields with a non-class structure type
Well yes, that's the requirement for instances as well (or rather implicit_reducibly instead of reducibly)

Eric Wieser said:

Maybe its worth doing some quick analysis of how many typeclasses have fields with a non-class structure type

It is not just about type classes with fields that are non-class structures. It is about any instance that is constructed using a non-class structure. For example docs#Equiv.field and docs#RingCon.instCommRingQuotient. When not used right, both of these will create instances with bad defeq properties.
Where "used correctly" for docs#Equiv.field means "either the Equiv is reducible, or the data instances are created manually and fast_instance% is used to inline them into the field structure"?
I'm not sure what "correctly" means for docs#RingCon.instCommRingQuotient, since the parameter is in the type anyway
The only potential problem with docs#RingCon.instCommRingQuotient is expecting docs#RingCon.Quotient to be reducibly defeq to docs#AddCon.Quotient.
That's never going to be true unless every RingCon declaration is itself reducible
It's never true, RingCon.Quotient and AddCon.Quotient are semireducible.
Oh, I assumed they were reducible and this came down to reducibility of toAddCon

Eric Wieser said:

Maybe its worth doing some quick analysis of how many typeclasses have fields with a non-class structure type

fwiw https://gist.github.com/matthewjasper/0a8a2e11f35b660f34673c629a310fc3 lists these (with some filtering).

Jireh Loreaux said:

Matthew Jasper said:

  • Rewrite the instances to use { RingHom.comp _ _ with toFun = _} and use Algebra.algebraMap directly.
  • Create implicit_reducible helper definitions that are otherwise the same as RingHom.comp,

I'm not sure what is the problem with either of these ideas. They both seem reasonable to me.

Sorry, I am behind on this thread. It seems viable to me to proceed with either, but the first,

Rewrite the instances to use { RingHom.comp _ _ with toFun = _} and use Algebra.algebraMap directly.

seems least confusing to me?

Shall we proceed on that basis?
I would like to propose a third option: we define a fast_structure% elaborator, and use that to reduce the RingHom to its constructors.

Or alternatively, we modify fast_instance% so that it doesn't complain if the thing it reduces is not an instance.

And then fast_instance% would need to do whnf in default transparency.
There's already delta%, but it doesn't unfold fields (and it's not consistent whether fields should be unfolded).
Yes, we need a version of delta% that recursively reduces the structure to its constructors.
Unfolding everything isn't what we want though.
We want to unfold all the way to the structure constructors. This is what fast_instance% does as well (but in the reducible_and_instances transparency)

As someone not really understanding most of these issues, I want to voice my concern that there soon might be inferInstance, fast_instance%, inferInstanceAs and maybe fast_structure which for me all seem to do similar things.

My fear as a mostly downstream user is using the wrong one im my projects and having stuff not work, not realizing it is because I'm using the wrong one.

I guess some beginner friendly documentation about these (why they are needed, when, when not, and why they are called fast:-) would already help, but I would also ask you to always consider if we need all of the subtlety, or if we can unify some of these.

Such commands add a real learning curve to the language :)

Sorry if this is just me being largely unaffected by these issues (probably because of all of the people's work here!) and not understanding the need for these special operators!
I highly appreciate all the work the people in this thread are doing, even if I don't understand most of it!
I hope this is just me being a little scared in my ignorance

Moritz Roos said:

Such commands add a real learning curve to the language :)

Yes, that's a good point - we should be trying to reduce the number of different special commands.

It should be possible to have a single command doing both of the current fast_instance% and my proposed new fast_structure%.

Thinking about this again, an easy fix is to mark the right definitions with @[implicit_reducible] so that they are reduced by type class search, e.g.RingHom.id and RingHom.comp. So in particular, this would mean tagging all .id and .comp definitions with @[implicit_reducible].

Somehow, I can't remember why we discarded this simple solution. I also can't imagine this causing performance problems.

I would need some progress on this front, to fix a bunch of diamonds related to R and C actions in #38451. The diamonds come from algebra actions, so what is relevant here is RingHom.comp (and not the other composition lemmas, because they don't show up in the typeclasses). I've tried making it implicit_reducible in #38315 and this gives a good performance improvement (-0.08%) contrary to my initial expectation. To me, this looks like a reasonable solution: whenever RingHom.comp shows up in an instance, it's likely we will need to unfold it if there are several competing ways to get to the instance, and otherwise implicit_reducible has no effect, so it can only make things better.

On the PR, @Eric Wieser asks for a principled solution. My suggestion would be: mark as implicit_reducible anything that solves instance diamonds. Another possibility that has been mentioned above is to define a function RingHom.implicitReducibleComp which is just like RingHom.comp but implicit reducible, and use that when defining things that show up in instances. But I don't see what it gains over a plain implicit_reducible attribute on RingHom.comp.

Thoughts?

Another candidate for implicit_reducible is RingHom.id, but it shows up a lot in linear algebra types and reducing it there could be costly for no gain, so I am not completely sure. I try this in #38509 to see the outcome.
There is no measurable loss, so I think it's reasonable to do. With that, we could remove the hack in the definition of docs#Algebra.id.
Yeah, I agree with this, especially if there is no performance loss.
We also need to do AddMonoidHom.id, because of Real.instRCLike.
Besides performance, the only other argument against implicit_reducible that I can think of is that we want to have different instances on the two forms, but for .id and .comp this does not apply.

It looks like Jovan and I agree here, but that's not enough to make progress, we would need another maintainer to push the button on #38315 for instance. @Eric Wieser, do you have concerns on this approach, or do you think it is a reasonable way to go?
Would it make sense to pre-emptively make all the .comps implicit_reducible? Is docs#Function.comp already so?
I think Function.comp should be, but it is in core :sweat_smile:
What I dislike about just changing the ring version is that this doesn't help current or future downstream projects that themselves have typeclasses containing morphisms
Yes, I agree, it would be better to try changing all of the .comp in one go and measuring performance.
If by any chance you're updating core's Function.comp, could you also make it dependent please? (i.e. merge docs#Function.dcomp into it)
That's a completely unrelated refactor
Indeed, and unrelated to the current thread (sorry!), but since changing core is sadly a slow process I thought it's worth mentioning

Eric Wieser said:

What I dislike about just changing the ring version is that this doesn't help current or future downstream projects that themselves have typeclasses containing morphisms

That's true of typeclasses containing anything complicated, there is nothing specific to morphisms here. If we have no typeclasses involving some objects in Mathlib, I would be surprised if they show up downstream. So I'm not convinced it's worth it. But the change also shouldn't cost anything if these compositions don't show up in typeclasses (precisely because they only change the transparency in instances), so I'm not opposed either, just neutral. I'm making the experiment in #38618, let's see what comes out of it.

The radar on #38618 is good, essentially the same as making RingHom.comp implicit-reducible, as expected. I'm sure I forgot some .comp, but the PR should handle most of them. If you see imporant ones that I'm missing, just tell me!

I conjecture that the slowdown in JacobiZariski can be easily fixed by a universe-renaming hack. I can check later, but I've seen this sort of thing before: you fiddle, JacobiZariski gets slower, turns out that it's just the kernel taking an inordinately large amount of time to typecheck a proof for reasons which it's very hard to diagnose because minimising is really difficult (I have had mathlib_minimiser running for literally months on such a minimisation and it's still not finished), and the changes just make things worse for reasons which are extremely difficult to diagnose, but which can all magically be fixed by renaming a universe from v to t or some other hack.

I already know what the big speedup is in Algebra.Category.CommAlgCat.Monoidal, again it will be just one declaration (specifically instance : BraidedCategory (CommAlgCat.{u} R)) which now is magically typechecking much faster again for reasons which are hard to diagnose: see https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/38315#issuecomment-4319553819

Yes, most of the speedup should be coming from making RingHom.comp implicit-reducible. #38315, which only makes that, has a speedup of 136.9G, while #38618 making everyone implicit-reducible has a speedup of 148.4G, so roughly the same. Fine-prints indeed differ, notably in JacobiZariski, but just like you I have learnt not to worry about this one.
Is there something more that is needed to get #38618 in?
